sections.markdown:

Robert is 65; Mary is entered with the Glasgow surname repeated by ditto and a Scotland birthplace mark. The schedule has no relationship column. These are readings of one census, not three independent family witnesses. A full original 1851 household and the 1839 marriage remain the discriminating identity tests.

The age conflict must be tested in the original schedule before transferring any identity or parentage. See the dated comparison below.

The copied 1841 household account places a Mary Glasgow, age 19, in Robert’s Holly Walk household. Household membership is positive contextual evidence, but the account supplies no relationship labels and the census page has not been independently inspected. Robertson-30564’s captured biography lists four children and does not name Mary; that summary’s omission does not prove she was not a daughter. sections.title: Father assessment — 24 October 2026
sections.markdown:
The captured WikiTree biography records Mary as born in 1804 in France and as a daughter of Robertson-30564 and Anne Glasgow-2874. Its only family evidence is a copied household note: in 1841 Robert Glasgow, age 65, of independent means, born in Scotland, lived at Holly Walk, Leamington Priors, with Ann Glasgow, 40; Mary Glasgow, 19; Ann Robertson, 18; Jane Robertson, 20; Charlotte Robertson, 10; and Wilhelmina Robertson, 1, plus servants. The note says Wilhelmina was the daughter of Robert’s eldest son, also Robert, but does not state the relationships of Mary, Ann Robertson, or Jane.

This co-residence supports keeping Mary as a possible daughter. The current Robertson-30564 profile summary lists Robert (1811), Philadelphia Jane, Anne, and Charlotte; it does not list Mary, but the list is a captured profile summary and its incompleteness is not a concrete contradiction. The age 19 in the copied household note would be inconsistent with a literal 1804 birth, but neither the profile date/place nor the copied age is verified here. The birth field remains unchanged and is not treated as an established conflict. The existing father claim is `C-1c3aef1700d1`, unmarked and without an individual previous percentage; citation evidence `E-964ef361dd20` is the copied household note.

The 45% assessment is subjective and reflects evidence for household association without a recorded parent role. No source here proves Mary’s identity as the household member or as a daughter. The existing WikiTree mother link to Anne Glasgow-2874 remains unassessed.

potential_parentage.method: Automated leads use birth surnames—not married surnames—as parental eligibility, role-specific biological age limits, bounded and approximate-date uncertainty, household chronology, specific time-aware localities, mapped distance, tenancy succession, migration destinations and sex-aware Scottish naming positions across generations. People already attached as the subject's parents stay in the identity summary and are excluded from this alternative-candidate list, regardless of relationship confidence. The main calibration uses clues available on disconnected profiles; existing parent and sibling links are retained as comparison context rather than treated as transferable evidence. Common ordered names and grandparent-to-child echoes receive a small non-zero weight, so a John or James match can support several independent criteria without producing a lead alone. Rare names, repeated bearers and bundles across otherwise distinct branches receive substantially more weight according to catalogue frequency. An exact migration place is weighted by its rarity and repetition across both branches; a shared destination country is worth only one point. Extra weight is added only when at least three independent clue types converge: naming, locality, specific migration, household chronology or collateral networks. Sparse profiles retain a clearly labelled chronology-only fallback instead of disappearing. Countries, states, counties and research clusters do not count as a shared locality, and fallback, broad representative or kin-inferred coordinates are excluded from distance scoring. Shared descendant profiles are removed before branch-name comparison. A candidate already recorded as a parent-in-law is excluded. A confident or independently supported parent is treated as settled; uncertain and unassessed attachments remain open to alternative comparison. A different linked parent, an uncle/aunt or grandparent path, and a matching existing child profile prevent an alternative from being classified as a strong direct-parent lead until the underlying tree conflict or duplicate is resolved. Familiar forms such as Bessie are normalised. Surname remains an eligibility filter worth zero points.
potential_parentage.warning: Naming customs, shared farms and occupations are circumstantial. Children, spouses and collateral relatives may be missing, and tree-derived family networks are not independent evidence. Scores rank research leads; they do not prove parentage.

position.answer: Original census review, 31 October 2026: The original 1841 Holly Walk census image has now been inspected through Findmypast: HO107/1135/14, folio 11, printed page 15, Leamington Priors. Robert is 65; Mary is entered with the Glasgow surname repeated by ditto and a Scotland birthplace mark. Mary’s final age digit remains ambiguous between 17 and 19: Findmypast transcribes 17, FreeCEN 19. Ann’s age also has an unresolved final digit (40/44; both providers transcribe 40). The schedule has no relationship column. These are readings of one census, not three independent family witnesses. The original does not prove Mary was Robert’s daughter or identify her with Mary Wilhelmina Campbell. record_associations.note: A specific daughter-in-law alternative can now be tested. Paterson’s 1866 county history, printed pp. 513–514 (PDF 249–250), says the elder Robert’s eldest son and heir, born 22 May 1811, married Mary-Wilhelmina, daughter of John Campbell of Stonefield, on 11 July 1839; their children include Wilhelmina-Colquhoun. The checked existing bride is Campbell-38211 and groom Robertson-Glasgow-11. A married Mary beside the infant of this same family could be that daughter-in-law rather than another daughter of the household head. This is a new comparison, not an established identification. The age problem remains real: FreeCEN gives Mary 19 in 1841, while Campbell-38211’s public profile gives 1816 and copies an 1851 age 34. The latter original is also unread. The infant’s full name and birth particulars are not established by FreeCEN. Paterson is a compiled family history, not an original marriage entry, and its adjacent Montgreenan descent narrative has known conflicts with the separately held court evidence. Do not transfer the book’s explicit John Campbell parentage to Glasgow-3021 before identifying the two Marys. Retain the selected Robert Robertson father at 45%, Jane’s father at 78%, all mother/vital fields and separate profiles; no father replacement, merge or confidence improvement is recorded. The volume title page (PDF19) reads1866; the host filename’s1863 date is misleading.
